newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: NATO, Russia seek agreement on future.
newsitem.headline: NATO, Russia seek agreement on future.

text.p: Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov, hoping to sweep away remaining obstacles to a Russia-NATO pact, arrived in Luxembourg on Tuesday for key talks on a new European security order.
"I am hoping for a successful meeting," he told reporters as he arrived at the airport for talks with NATO Secretary General Javier Solana.
The two men are to meet at a secluded chateau outside the town centre at 7 p.m. (1700 gmt).

The Western allies want a charter or "document", which gives Moscow a permanent consultative role with its old Cold War enemy, to form the centrepiece of a new security order in Europe and alleviate Russian concerns over the alliance's planned eastwards enlargement.

Moscow strongly opposes likely NATO membership for Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic and wants strong commitments from NATO setting clear limits on military activities in the new members. NATO says such demands are out of the question because such issues are a matter of sovereignty.

NATO, which is keen to clinch a deal with Russia ahead of its planned enlargement into eastern Europe, has played down suggestions the meeting in Luxembourg could lead to a breakthrough on a host of outstanding military issues.
Primakov told reporters in Strasbourg on Monday he hoped to complete a draft agreement at the Luxembourg talks.
"I want this meeting to be the last one and to enable us to sign on May 27. The possibility of signing the document will be totally cleared up tomorrow," he said.
President Boris Yeltsin has said he wants to sign the new deal at a special summit on May 27 in Paris.

NATO officials, fearing the Russians are trying to rush NATO countries into fudging the last few points, say it may be possible by then but it is not certain that all differences can be narrowed in time.
Primakov repeated Moscow's ritual denunciation of NATO plans to admit former Soviet bloc central European countries as "the most serious error since the end of the Cold War".
But he added that a Russia-NATO document should minimise the repercussions on Russian security.

Alliance officials said Primakov was talking up the meeting as a "last-chance" attempt to clinch a deal in the hope of winning some minor extra concessions from NATO, which says it has nothing left to offer.

NATO, which says enlargement will begin whatever Russia says at a summit in Madrid next July, has offered Moscow a permanent Russia-NATO consultative council and pledged not to station troops or weapons on the territory of the new members.

Russia has demanded the new members not be permitted to overhaul existing military establishments, such as airfields, to bring them in line with NATO standards and wants NATO to pledge "never" to extend its military umbrella eastwards.
"Such assurances would impinge on the sovereignty of new members and create a second-class membership. That is unacceptable," said one NATO official.
Last week, U.S. and Russian officials said progress was made at talks in Moscow between Primakov and U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright but the essential problems remained unresolved.

NATO sources said the Russian side made some concessions over the related issue of changes to the 1990 Conventional Forces in Europe (CFE) treaty -- one of the key post-Cold War accords limiting numbers of weapons and where they can be placed.

NATO wants to scrap group ceilings for force levels in favour of purely national ceilings, but Russia wants to retain them. NATO demands the right to station some foreign forces in other countries but Russia rejects this.
